idiom_name: swift-syntax SyntaxVisitor/SyntaxRewriter (visitAny, visitPost) over a source-accurate tree
implementation_notes: SwiftSyntax provides the tree and the engine for real Swift source: SyntaxVisitor subclasses override visitX methods (or visitAny on SyntaxAnyVisitor) and return SyntaxVisitorContinueKind to decide whether to descend, while SyntaxRewriter subclasses override visitAny and return replacement syntax or nil to keep the node and continue - so the walk belongs to the base class and the pattern plus action live in the override. Nodes are value types (Syntax, ExprSyntax, DeclSyntax) with typed accessors and as? casts for structural tests, and rebuilds keep the parent chain consistent; SwiftSyntaxBuilder helps construct replacements. For a tree you own, a plain indirect enum with switch patterns over associated values plus a recursive function is the lighter form of the same idea; the package is the right choice whenever the subject is actual Swift syntax (it is also the backbone of the macro system).
pitfalls: Returning a replacement from too general a check in visitAny short-circuits the subtree's normal dispatch, so patterns must be narrow and fall back to nil; read-only rules should use SyntaxVisitor instead of a rewriter.

SwiftSyntax nodes are value types with parent pointers maintained by the library, so a replacement built from scratch has a different identity and parent chain, which breaks equality checks and source-range assumptions.

Node type names change between swift-syntax majors (the infix expression nodes in particular), so the package version must be pinned - a rule written against older node names stops compiling after an upgrade.
